Description: The Púkel-men are described inconsistently within the same paragraph. First they are said to be 'huge and clumsy-limbed, squatting cross-legged with their stumpy arms folded on fat bellies' with 'all features' worn away except 'dark holes of their eyes,' and the Riders heed them little with 'no power or terror left in them.' Yet immediately after, 'strange runes gleamed faintly upon the Púkel-men, drawing Merry's gaze, for they were fair of form and thrummed with a power both ancient and dreadful.' This directly contradicts the earlier description—they cannot simultaneously be featureless, clumsy, powerless stone figures AND fair of form with thrumming ancient dreadful power.

Bilbo gives Frodo his mithril-coat and Sting, forgetting he had already done so. However, this is not actually an error—Bilbo's forgetfulness is explicitly noted in the text as a character trait due to his great age. The narrative intentionally shows his memory failing. Upon closer reading, this is a deliberate portrayal of Bilbo's decline, not a narrative error.

Bilbo gives Frodo Sting and the mithril-coat again in Rivendell, but these were already given to Frodo in Lothlórien in Chapter 21 according to the previous summaries. The summary for Chapter 21 states 'Bilbo gives Frodo Sting and his mithril coat' before the Company departs Rivendell. However, checking the actual text of this chapter, Bilbo is in Rivendell and gives these items to Frodo before Frodo leaves for the Shire. The previous summary for Chapter 16 mentions Bilbo giving Frodo Sting and mithril coat before departing Rivendell the first time. This creates a contradiction—Bilbo gives these items twice, once before the Fellowship departs and once when Frodo returns. But the text explicitly notes Bilbo 'forgetting that he had already done so,' which accounts for this. This is intentional characterization, not an error.

Treebeard says 'But not Ents. There are no Entings.' Yet earlier in Chapter 27, Merry and Pippin learned from Treebeard about the Ents and Entwives, and Treebeard's search for them. The lack of Entings is consistent with this established lore. However, Treebeard also says 'Forests may grow. Woods may spread. But not Ents.' This seems contradictory to Aragorn's statement 'Yet maybe there is now more hope in your search'—but this is Aragorn offering hope, not a statement of fact. Upon review, this is not an error but thematic consistency about the Ents' decline.

In Chapter 12, Frodo was stabbed in the shoulder by the Witch-king with a Morgul-knife. In this chapter, Strider states that 'all blades perish that pierce that dreadful King,' implying Frodo's sword made contact and wounded the Witch-king. However, in the previous chapter's attack, Frodo put on the Ring, saw the Ringwraiths clearly, and was stabbed while invisible—there is no indication he successfully struck the Witch-king with his sword. The slash in the cloak is presented as new information here, but the previous chapter described Frodo falling unconscious after being stabbed without any mention of him drawing his sword or striking a blow. This creates a contradiction in the sequence of events during the Weathertop attack.

Gandalf says he passed through Moria and came out alive, and later says he came from the East, yet he also says he does not know the opening word to the West-gate and has never entered that way. However, he also says 'I have not spoken of it to the Company before' and 'Aragorn was against it, until the pass over the mountains had at least been tried,' implying he had considered Moria as a route from the beginning. The inconsistency is that if Gandalf came from the East through Moria, he would not need to enter through the West-door and would not know its password, which is consistent; but his claim to have 'passed through' and 'come out again alive' suggests a complete traversal, which would require entering from one side and exiting the other. If he only exited from the East, he didn't truly 'pass through' in the sense of traversing the entire mines. This is a minor semantic inconsistency in his description of his experience.

Sam reaches to grab water-skins from 'the table beside him' while they are hiding in brambles under a rock-face in the wilderness of Mordor. There is no table present in their hiding place, making this a physical impossibility.

Frodo gives Sting to Sam, saying 'Sting I give to you. I have got an orc-blade.' However, in the previous chapter (Chapter 55 summary), Sam already had Sting and used it to fight Shelob and the orcs. The narrative in Chapter 55 states Sam 'wounded the giant spider with Sting,' and he carried Sting throughout Frodo's captivity. This chapter treats the transfer of Sting as happening now, when it logically should have occurred earlier or Sam already possessed it.

Merry claims the ponies belong to him ('Merry, to whom the others belonged'), but earlier in Chapter 6, the ponies were acquired for the journey by Merry's preparations at Crickhollow, and in Chapter 7, the hobbits entered the Old Forest on foot without ponies. The ponies were left behind at the Forest's edge or at Crickhollow. Tom Bombadil somehow retrieved them after rescuing the hobbits from Old Man Willow, but the ownership claim and how Tom obtained them is muddled—Merry didn't bring his own ponies into the Forest, and the text earlier suggests they were borrowed or arranged for the journey, not personally owned by Merry.

The text describes the Balrog as having 'a sense of serenity and gentle joy' emanating from it, which directly contradicts the established nature of Balrogs as demons of terror and shadow. This appears to be a corrupted or mistaken description, as the Balrog is immediately afterward described with fire, shadow, and menace, and all characters react with terror. The 'serenity and gentle joy' is completely inconsistent with both the Balrog's nature and the narrative context.

Aragorn states he sent Boromir to follow Merry and Pippin, but there is no previous indication of this arrangement. Earlier in the chapter, Aragorn was separately tracking Frodo's footprints on the hill while Boromir was apparently with the hobbits. The statement contradicts the narrative flow where Aragorn went up the hill alone and Boromir was left with the hobbits without any explicit command from Aragorn to follow Merry and Pippin specifically.

Merry states that five months ago corresponds to five nights ago, which is mathematically impossible. If five months have passed, it cannot be only five nights ago. This appears to be a conflation of different timeframes or a character error that creates confusion.

Pippin mentions that Treebeard told them all about Moria, implying this conversation happened when they first met. However, in the previous chapter (Chapter 27), Merry and Pippin told their tale to Treebeard, not the other way around. Treebeard already knew about Gandalf's fall in Moria from the hobbits' account, which explains why he wasn't surprised to see Gandalf alive—but Pippin's statement reverses the information flow.

Frodo says he has 'never even considered the direction' he must go, yet immediately before this he had already decided to go to Rivendell with Gandalf's advice, and even earlier in the conversation he says 'I go to lose one, and not return, as far as I can see'—showing he had indeed been thinking about where he was going. The claim that he never considered direction contradicts his active engagement in planning his journey.

In Chapter 3, Gandalf explicitly tells Frodo 'Do not use it!' regarding the Ring, warning him of its dangers. However, in this chapter, when Frodo feels the desire to use the Ring to hide from the Black Rider, he thinks 'The advice of Gandalf seemed absurd. Bilbo had used the Ring.' This misrepresents Gandalf's advice—Gandalf never suggested using the Ring was acceptable, he strictly forbade it. Frodo's internal thought that Gandalf's advice was to not use it (implying it was merely advisory rather than imperative) and his comparison to Bilbo's usage distorts the actual warning from the previous chapter.
The text contains a malformed word 'would'' with an extra apostrophe before 'not' - appears to be a typographical error that creates incoherence.
The text contains a malformed word 'wen' instead of 'were' in the description of Dúnedain marriage customs.
The text contains a malformed word 'mat' instead of 'that' in Ivorwen's prophecy.
The text contains a malformed word 'be' instead of 'he' in the description of Ar-Pharazôn's counsel.
The text contains a malformed word 'bad' instead of 'had' in the description of the Great Armament.

Faramir recoils from Éowyn with scorn and no warmth passes between them, which directly contradicts the immediately preceding romantic proposal and acceptance, as well as the subsequent description of them walking 'hand in hand' with 'light that shone about them.' The text abruptly inserts hostile physical and emotional reactions that are inconsistent with the narrative arc of their reconciliation and betrothal.
